note.question: What role does conditional lead-time flexibility play in an assemble-to-order system?
note.overview: We introduce and formalize a concept termed conditional lead-time flexibility (CLF), which refers to the industry practice where a manufacturer requests that its upstream suppliers dynamically adjust the pipeline orders’ remaining lead times. Over a finite horizon, an assemble-to-order manufacturer makes joint decisions on inventory replenishment and lead-time adjustment to minimize the total discounted expected cost. The problem is formulated as a multiperiod dynamic programming with an enlarged state space to track the adjustable pipeline orders.

source.quote: To facilitate the understanding of how conditional lead-time flexibility works and its impact on the inven­ tory decisions, in this section, we incorporate CLF into the simplest ATO system with one key component and one product.
The manufacturer manages the ATO system by procuring the key component from the supplier and assembling it into the product.
The manufacturer manages the ATO system by procuring the key component from the supplier and assembling it into the product.

Markov Decision Process Formulation and Decomposition The manufacturer faces the following sequence of events in period t. (1) Receive the shipment that is due. (2) Observe the system state yt. (3) Decide the ordering quan­ tity zt ≥0. (4) Observe the realized CLF St. (5) Adjust yt to ˆyt ∈F(yt,St). (6) Observe the realized demand dt. (7) Assess all the costs.

Because the supplier has the autonomy to flexibly determine the set of adjustment boundaries based on her production capacity, raw materials, and workforce, St is random from the manufacturer’s perspective.

(4) When would be better to take the route of CLF rather than dual sourcing or triple sourcing?
